Trace the evolution of a robust feature descriptor from a raw patch to orientation-normalized spatial histograms, explaining each step's shortcoming.
risposta: A raw image patch matches exactly but is highly sensitive to brightness and position changes. Using image gradients adds invariance to brightness shifts but remains sensitive to rotation, deformation, and contrast (motivating normalization). A color histogram is invariant to rotation/scale but discards all spatial layout, making it non-discriminative. Spatial histograms (per-cell, as in HOG/SIFT) restore some layout and are partially invariant to small deformations, but the fixed spatial bins make them sensitive to rotation. Finally, orientation normalization aligns the patch to its dominant gradient orientation before computing the descriptor, achieving full rotation invariance.

domanda: Explain the three histogram comparison measures and their relative robustness.
risposta: Histogram intersection sums min(qi,vi) over bins, measuring the shared part of two histograms, and is robust. Euclidean (L2) distance, sqrt(sum (qi-vi)^2), is simple but weighs all bins equally and is not very robust. Chi-square distance, sum (qi-vi)^2/(qi+vi), weighs bins differently and is more discriminative, making it a stronger choice for comparing histogram descriptors.

domanda: Describe the full HOG pipeline for pedestrian detection and state its key properties.
risposta: HOG combines gradients, spatial cells, and local contrast normalization on a fixed patch (e.g. 64x128). (1) Gradient computation: per-pixel magnitude and unsigned orientation in 0-180 degrees. (2) Cell histograms: divide into 8x8 cells, build a 9-bin orientation histogram per cell where each pixel votes weighted by its magnitude, with bilinear interpolation between bins to avoid aliasing. (3) Block normalization: group cells into 2x2 blocks, concatenate and normalize (v/sqrt(||v||^2+eps)) for contrast robustness, with overlapping blocks so interior cells contribute multiple times. (4) Feature vector: concatenate normalized blocks (e.g. 3780-dim for 64x128), fed to a linear SVM. HOG is single-scale and has no dominant orientation, so it suits canonical-pose objects like upright pedestrians and is not rotation invariant.
